title: Don't be turned into a Caesar
hookLine: beware of becoming an emperor inside; stay simple, kind, unaffected (Meditations 6.30)

lines: DON'T BE TURNED INTO A CAESAR.
cards: Day two hundred. A coworker got promoted, and changed, a little at a time. They started saying we at the leadership level.
They stopped eating lunch with the old team. Their jokes got less funny and everyone laughed harder.
It can happen to anyone with a little power: the team lead, the head of the committee, the person with a few thousand followers. Marcus had the throne itself. And he watched himself for exactly this.

teach.h: TAKE CARE: NOT MADE INTO A CAESAR.
teach.b: Here's how Book Six, section thirty, begins in George Long's translation: "Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye." Then three small words: for such things happen.
Remember the dye from a week ago? The soul is dyed by the thoughts. Here Marcus fears one particular color, the color of being emperor, soaking in until it's all the way through.
In the Greek, some readers think he made up a word for it, something like: don't get Caesared. Being called Caesar was his job. He's afraid of Caesar becoming who he is.
The cure is a list for himself: stay simple, good, pure, serious, free from showing off, a friend of justice, reverent toward the gods, kind, affectionate, and strong in doing what's right.

Then he holds up the man who raised him to the throne, his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius: how steady he was, how gentle, how little he cared for empty fame, how carefully he listened, how he never rushed a decision, content with plain food and a plain bed.
Be his pupil still, Marcus tells himself. Life is short. There is only one fruit of this life, he says: a reverent disposition and acts for the common good.

You probably aren't about to be made an emperor. But everyone gets some little throne: a title, a role, a bit of being needed. The question is whether it stays a job or becomes a costume you can't take off.

how: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own roles and titles, and many traditions have practices of humility for people in positions of power.

o: letting a role soak in until it's who you are
betrayed and stabbed by the friends you trusted
being crowned ruler after winning a great war

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: the one fruit of this life

s: Marcus was afraid of losing the throne
he was afraid of the throne changing who he was, dyeing him through.
Marcus held up his adoptive father as his model
Antoninus Pius: steady, gentle, careless of empty fame, content with plain things.
Marcus wrote that such things happen
'for such things happen': he knew the role could dye him through.

games.q: you're Marcus, emperor of Rome. you notice the role changing you. what do you do?
o: write yourself a list and remember the man who raised you.
games.why: he lists what to stay (simple, good, kind) and holds up Antoninus Pius as the picture to follow.

practice: Notice which little throne you sit on: a title, being the one who knows, the busy one, the one people come to. Imagine setting it on the floor for these two minutes. Underneath it is just a person breathing; rest as that person.

wordCard.voice: Caesared. Marcus's rare word for being turned into a Caesar, letting the role dye him through instead of staying simple, good and kind. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: from Marcus's warning 'don't be Caesared', a rare word; some readers think Marcus coined it.

carryVoice: Your line: stay simple. A title is a job, not who you are. Two hundred days in, and thank you for every one.

sources.q: Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye
